I am 56 years old, middle school educated, and I have been farming these 2 mu in Quzhou County for 37 years. My wife and I manage the land while our child works in a factory in the city, so there are only two of us for labor and we cannot hire help — every yuan must be counted. On a plot this small, growing grain barely covers costs, so chili is our best choice because the Shandong buyers come through Quzhou every autumn and the price is steady. I know this sandy-loam soil well, and our well gives reliable water, though pumping costs money so I irrigate only when the crop really needs it.

This year I will put the full 2 mu into hybrid chili. I thought about using my own saved seeds, but the hybrid seedlings from the agro-shop in town give fatter pods and resist disease better, and for only 2 mu the extra seed cost is manageable. In late March I will rotary till the ground and lay plastic mulch to warm the soil — that is what my neighbor Old Wang does and his chili always comes out strong. For fertilizer, I will spread farmyard manure first, then apply about 15 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 10 kg of potassium per mu. I split it: base dressing before transplanting, then a top-dress of urea and potassium sulfate when the flowers start showing. The extension agent says 15 kg N is enough, but two years ago I tried that and the leaves yellowed too early, so I learned to stick with this amount. I will irrigate four times: once before transplanting the seedlings in early April, then at flowering, during fruit set, and once more in late summer if the rains fail. I will spray pesticide four times, mainly for aphids and the black spot disease that comes with our humid summers — I buy the generic bottles from the village store, they work fine. I expect about 1,100 kg of fresh chili per mu if the weather holds; that is a bit less than what the big farms advertise, but with our own labor on 2 mu it is honest, stable income.
